Mr. Speaker, may I inquire of the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) if he intends to proceed with Bill No. 24, an act to define Canadian nationals?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) very courteously gave me notice that he intended to ask this question, and I desire to make the following statement:
I regret that we will be unable to proceed, during the present session, with Bill No. 24, entitled "An Act to define Canadian nationals and to provide for loss or renunciation of Canadian nationality."
I think that the underlying principles of that bill meet with the general approval of this house. There is an increasing demand for such legislation from all Canadian religious organizations, which have missionaries in foreign countries; from Canadian commercial and industrial companies, which maintain agencies in other countries for the develop-

Inquiries for Returns

ment of their overseas trade; and from representatives and agents of the dominion and provincial governments, who, necessarily, reside outside of Canada. They all desire that provision should be made in our statutes whereby they and their families while residing abroad, may retain their status as Canadian nationals, and maintain their permanent domicile in Canada, though temporarily resident abroad while representing in other countries Canada and Canadian institutions.
Obviously, they also desire to have and to maintain the right for themselves and their families to return from time to time to Canada to visit their principals and their relatives and their friends, and, when deemed desirable, to resume their permanent residence in Canada.
To assure Canadian nationals of this right will require certain amendments and modifications of our existing immigration laws. Inasmuch as the Minister of Immigration is now constantly engaged as chairman of the special committee which is investigating the Beau-harnois project, it has been deemed expedient to postpone, for this session, further consideration of Bill No. 24, which has passed its second reading in this house, in the hope that some satisfactory compromise may be reached in respect of the amendments of the existing immigration laws, which should be made to protect fully the rights and interests of Canadian nationals and their families who are resident abroad and who may desire to resume their permanent domicile in Canada.

speechtext: He joined the force as a young man of twenty-two years of age and has now served continuously over a period of forty-six years. Since 1923 he has been in command of the force. He has at all times given most excellent and most efficient service.

I would also announce
that his position has been filled by the appointment of Major-General MacBrien, to become effective on the first day of August next. General MacBrien commenced his military career as a constable in the Northwest Mounted Police. He has in that way had a great deal of experience in regard to police work. Subsequently he entered the permanent force of Canada and rose to a very high position as a military commander during the late war, and is to-day undoubtedly one of the most outstanding military men that this country has produced. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not improbable that hon. members, especially those who reside in western Canada, may be interested to know that the government, in view of the situation which obtains, has concluded to direct the purchase of 2,000,000 bushels of wheat, which will be ground into flour by the mills of the west, thereby enabling the municipalities and those requiring assistance to obtain flour at a very reasonable price. Where distribution has to be made, we will be in a position to do so without delay. This will produce approximately 450,000 barrels of flour, and the bran and shorts remaining also will be available if so desired. I mention this at once in order that hon. members who may be receiving communications from municipalities and other parts of the west may be able to reassure those who are so directly affected by the drought conditions in their provinces.

Customs tariff-6. Live hogs, per pound: British preferential tariff, free; intermediate tariff, lj cents; general tariff, 3 cents.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The committee will perhaps recall that since some of the items between item 2 and item 48 were affected by the Australian treaty items, we began with item 54a. We are now taking up the items from item 2 to item 54a, and the item under consideration is item 6.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The request for this increase came .from western Canada; various members representing western constituencies, as well as others interested in farming operations, believed that the tariff did not afford them that protection from unfair competition which is so desirable, and the item is being changed to free, II cents and 3 cents.

I presume the demand for protection is based on the supposition that large numbers of hogs have been shipped into Canada; I imagine that is the only basis there could be for such a request. It would be very interesting for the committee to know just exactly what has been the importation of live hogs, and I have taken the trouble to look up the statistics covering importations from the United States for the last four years. I have assumed that live hogs imported would run about 200 pounds per hog; the figures are given in pounds, and therefore I have taken them on that basis. In 1928 there were 2.802 pounds imported, which would mean about 14 hogs. It is true that in 1929 the imports

were a little larger; they amounted to 110,885 pounds, which at 200 pounds per hog would mean about 550 or a few more hogs. In 1930 the imports were 2,523 pounds, or 12 hogs, or a little more, and in 1931, 7,649 pounds, or about 38 hogs. That is to say, during the last four years, on this basis, the numbers would be 38, 14, 550 and 12. So that even the greatest number, 550, is so insignificant in comparison with the hogs produced in Canada that it is hardly worth while using printers' ink to make the change. Sometimes these demands for increases in duties come from people who do not know the facts, and I am sure that the representatives of western agricultural interests who made this demand for an increased duty on live hogs were simply not aware of the situation. This is not a matter of producing more revenue; it is not even a question of giving protection to the farmers. The increase is made simply for the purpose of fooling tihe farmers who allow themselves to be fooled. Let me point out to. western members who are so anxious to have so-called protection on agricultural products that this is something which appears to give protection to the farmer while in reality it affords no protection at all. What do 12 hogs amount to, or 14, or even 550, the greatest number in the last four years, in comparison with the large number of hogs produced and slaughtered in Canada? This is in reality a duty to fool the farmers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Representations in connection with this item have been made to

the house. I have received letters from concerns in the province of Quebec which are interested in the manufacture of candles, in connection with which they use a certain amount of beeswax. Two of these letters I will read in the French language
(Translation): J.-C. Frenette, of Quebec, has sent me the following letter, dated June 18, 1931:
Together with other candle manufacturers I wish to protest against this increase in this tariff item from 7J to 20 per cent, on beeswax.
It is unnecessary to repeat the reasons given by my fellow-manufacturers, however, may I state that I entirely agree with their request not to alter the tariff, at least on beeswax imported by candle manufacturers. This protection of 20 per cent will in no way benefit beekeepers or wax-bleachers, because they cannot supply us with the special product required in our industry.
Trusting that the request of the candle manufacturers will be granted, I beg of you to accept my sincere thanks.
J.-C. Frenette,
(sgd.) I. Hardy.
J.-B. Lasnier, Inc., of Levis, is another company which manufactures candles and utilizes beeswax. This company contends that the proposed changes to the tariff would really be detrimental to its trade. The following letter was forwarded to me by this company on June 18, 1931:
We wish to protest, together with other candle manufacturers, against this uncalled for increase of 300 per cent in the tariff of beeswax, from 7J per cent for the intermediary tariff, to 20 per cent for the general tariff, which changes have been in force since June 1, the date of the budget statement.
This increase probably made at the request of the Beekeepers Association of Canada, at the suggestion of the Ruddy Mfg. Co. of Brantford (Ontario) will in no way benefit this association or the Canadian wax-bleachers, and it will not have the results expected; namely, to oblige candle-makers to purchase their supply of beeswax in Canada; on the contrary it will hinder our industry which already has to compete with foreign industries and particularly those of the United States; it will bring about a proportional increase in the price of candles in Canada, and will the more accentuate this competition.
Our churches already much in need of money, and as a whole, the congregation already otherwise taxed, will have to meet this increase without any compensation forthcoming to whomsoever.
The candle manufacturers will continue to purchase their supplies from the same source, because they exclusively utilize pure beeswax, bleached by the sun and air, and that special product cannot be supplied to them by the Canadian beeswax bleachers, because the summer, being the only season when this operation can be carried on is too short, the changes in temperature too frequent and sudden, and therefore detrimental to this work. This exposes the wax-bleachers to great losses. The other bleaching processes, whether chemical, mechanical or electrical, principally the

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
latter, used by the Ruddy Mfg. Co. has the great defect of extracting the fat ingredient which renders it unsuitable for the making of candles, a defect which we were able to ascertain because, with the hope of encouraging this new industry, we made purchases from this company. However, the poor results obtained from their products force us to discontinue placing further orders with this firm.
May we further add that the Ruddy Mfg. Co. take advantage of this tariff increase to unfairly raise their price by some cents per pound when the market for beeswax is down and does not seem to pick up.
We place these facts before you in the hope that the tariff will not be raised, at least in respect to beeswax, which is imported by candle manufacturers. France seems to be the country which lends itself best to the bleaching of beeswax by the sun and air and the tariff of 71 per cent should not be changed.
Kindly accept our sincere thanks.
(Sgd.) J.-B. Lasnier, Sr. Inc.
per Alf T.
In view of these representations I think this item should not pass.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member in his presentation of this case has fallen far short of my expectations.
He always does.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am rather surprised
that he has not made in this committee the presentation of the case which some of his colleagues made by circulars which were sent throughout the province of Quebec. I am rather astounded that he has not seen fit to assert that my hand is against the church, as has been stated in the circulars. I am rather amazed that it has not been said that in enacting this section I was acting for the Imperial Oil and the Standard Oil companies. That was said in the circulars, so why was it not said here? I have before me the circular put out by my hon. friends opposite in which it has been indicated that the tax on beeswax was a direct effort on the part of this man Bennett to make it more difficult to conduct services in the church, and that the price of candles would be greatly increased by reason of his action.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I never signed that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was stated that my
purpose was to improve the Imperial Oil and Standard Oil enterprises. Let me hasten to assure the committee that such is not the case. I fancy that very few people have been misled by such statements but I desire to avail myself of this opportunity-I thank my hon. friend for providing the opportunity -to make a denial to the committee. I cannot hope that the same publicity will be given to the denial as has been given to the unfounded statements, but one becomes
accustomed to almost any form of attack. Imagine an attack as far fetched as to make such assertions when the beekeepers of Canada, in convention assembled, producing as they do very large quantities of wax, have suggested that they should be given a little more opportunity to carry on their business under fair competition. This industry has assumed great proportions and when we met their suggestions it was circulated amongst the confiding and faithful people that this action was being taken to strike a blow at the mother church.

speakerposition: Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I never said that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is politics as practised by my hon. friends opposite. This is one item in which an increase has been made in the British preferential tariff. The rates have been increased from free to 15 per cent, from 7| to 20 per cent and from 10 to 20 per cent. The proportion of beeswax entering into the manufacture of candles is not very great. I think hon. members know something of the enormous development which has taken place in this industry. In looking over the figures of production a few weeks ago I was amazed to find that the industry has assumed great proportions in every province of Canada. In the province from whence I come the production of honey has reached a figure which a few years ago would have been thought impossible. It is so in all the provinces. The gentleman, Mr. Baillargeon, is a manufacturer of candles. He has communicated his position to the department. He gave evidence before the tariff advisory board in connection with an application for increased protection on candles. Perhaps the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Young) will recall the testimony and the application. We believe, in taking the course we have pursued, we have done something that will be of incalculable benefit to a very large number of people in every portion of every province of Canada; its application is not limited to one. I again assure my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) that when he replies to the communications that have been directed to him, he may give the most solemn assurance that there is no desire or intention on the part of that legendary figure, by name Bennett, that is being held up to the view of the confiding people of Quebec, in any way to interfere with the use of candles in churches, to increase their cost or to increase the profits of any refining company in the world.

What was the importation of beeswax last year? I assume that this

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
is a laudable attempt upon the part of the government to maintain a high standard of living amongst our Canadian working bees.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Importations to the value of $76,000.

I have listened with great interest to the remarks of the Prime Minister about beeswax. The duty on this commodity has been increased 200 per cent under the intermediate tariff and 100 per cent under the general tariff. Under the old tariff schedule the general rate was 10 per cent whereas now it is 20 per cent. Beeswax is a raw product which is used in the manufacture of candles, but it has to be bleached before it is so used. It has been said that beeswax is mostly used in candle manufacturing. May I say that 60 per cent of the candles that are used in Canada are made of paraffin; 40 per cent with the proportion of 60 per cent of beeswax and the balance other products, such as paraffin and acid. In order to manufacture high class candles, the beeswax has to be bleached, and I have been informed that on account of climatic conditions beeswax cannot be property bleached in this country. The Chemical process of bleaching beeswax for candle making has not been a success, and it has not given any satisfaction. Therefore the candle manufacturers have to import their beeswax mostly from Europe. Two hundred thousand pounds h'ave been imported from France and Belgium and 40,000 pounds from England.
Sixty per cent of the domestic production of beeswax is used, or I might say, re-used in the honey-making industry, so that whatever balance is offered on the market is far from being sufficient to meet the Canadian demand for beeswax for candle-making, and this is the reason why so much is imported. At present there is a tariff of 25 per cent on manufactured candles, and this has not been touched. If there is an increase in the tariff on beeswax which is one of the primary products to be used in the manufacture of candles, and if the tariff on manufactured candles is to remain as at present, what is going to be the result? It will most likely be that candles will be imported from the United States. There will be no protection whatever and in this way the industry of candle-making in this country will be greatly affected. Therefore the committee should decide that this tariff should not be increased because it will not benefit the honey industry and it will not benefit the candle-makers; the duty on manufactured candles remaining

at 25 per cent, importation of the finished product will result. More than half a million dollars of capital is invested in the candlemaking industry of Canada and therefore the old rate of duty of 10 per cent on beeswax should remain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I might say to my hon. friend that it was the Honey Producers Association and the Beekeepers' Association, national organizations, that pressed for this. The duty on beeswax in the United States is 30 per cent.

It may be that the honey producers might ask for some further protection so that they might be able to sell their products a little dearer, but have they proved that the bleaching of their beeswax has been successful in this country? It is acknowledged that owing to climatic conditions beeswax cannot be properly bleached in Canada in order to be used in making high quality candles to the satisfaction of the candle manufacturers, and as long as this raw product cannot be properly treated for use in making the finished product, I do not see that a higher tariff will in any way protect the honey industry.
I should like to inform the hon. gentleman that a good quality of bleached beeswax is being produced in the factory of the Ruddy Manufacturing Company in the city of Brantford.

The Ruddy Manufacturing Company may have asked for protection, but I have under my hand letters which I shall read to the committee showing that since the duty has been increased, they have increased their price three cents per pound on beeswax. 1 have other letters from candle manufacturers stating that their product is not giving entire satisfaction. I think we can, if no untoward event occurs, look forward to the most friendly administration of this treaty, and the fact that article nine appears in the document is in itself some evidence that that is the purpose and intent of both parties.

We are going to get into a somewhat complex situation, Mr. Chairman, if we are going to discuss the Australian treaty in connection with these items. But now that the subject has been introduced, might I say with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster that when he used the word "dumping" perhaps he did not mean it in the legal sense. The Prime Minister said that there was nothing to prevent dumping under the treaty. As long as eggs can be brought in from Australia during the months of January and February-those are the flood months of production in Australia-there is nothing to prevent enormous quantities being brought in and put in cold storage, and that, of course, would affect our market the whole year around. But as I say, perhaps that had better be considered when the Australian treaty is before us. But certainly that point is there, unless of course, you are going to specify that eggs brought in during January and February are laid in the month of January and February, which it would be practically impossible to do. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says that those are the months in which eggs can be brought in with the least interference with the Canadian poultry keepers. I would say to the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) that during recent yeans South Africa, including Rhodesia has so increased the export of oranges to Great Britain that last year they sent nearly one million cases. I took some little trouble to investigate the condition of the fruit coming in from South Africa, and I was amazed at what I found:. Modem cold storage facilities have been so improved as to permit the ready movement of fruit provided the proper precooling steps are taken when the fruit is taken from the tree. The fruit is delivered to the ships under conditions which have become a matter of scientific exactitude and it is delivered in London in an amazingly good condition. I did not think it possible that fruit could travel such .great distances and be delivered in such excellent condition, but it is being done.
Our friends in Australia, as do our friends in South Africa, feel quite confident that with the opening of this market to them so freely, they can develop a considerable trade. Orange juice has to some extent been superseded by tomato juice in the public use, but it is believed that this step will result in a great stimulus to the production of oranges within the empire and greatly improve our present position. Those who have tasted the oranges produced in the West Indies and Jamaica are amazed at the quality. I do not pose as an expert, but I do say that the oranges from South Africa appear to me to be as fine in flavour as any I have been privileged to eat. This is an experiment in the development of empire trade, and from the evidence before us, we believe it will be successful.
I am going to surprise my right hon. friend by telling him that I am in favour of this item.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That statement delights me greatly but it makes me fear that I may be wrong.

I had the opportunity of investigating the possibilities of increasing not only the quantity but the quality of oranges imported from Jamaica. A policy of this kind will certainly encourage interempire trade. It is the same principle under

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
which we raised the duty by 50 cents per stem on bananas under the general tariff, and allowed them to come in free under the British preferential.

This is the only item in the whole tariff where a duty is charged on the cubic measurement. This commodity will come in mostly by vessel, and ocean rates are charged on that basis. We should have a box which could be calculated easily as to cubic measurement, or else we will have trouble with the people handling these goods. There will not be two customs officials in the whole country who will measure these boxes alike, and a change should be made for the benefit of the traders of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The administration has not been found to be difficult nor is it believed that it will become more difficult because this happens to be the standard or yardstick of measurement provided for in the treaty.

I would like to enter a protest against an increased duty on oranges. Thousands of cases of this fruit are used in the hospitals in order to furnish drinks to the patients, thousands of doctors prescribe the juice of the orange for practically every patient they have and it is about the last thing that should be singled out for an increase. Orange juice is practically a medicine and it is needed by many people who cannot afford to buy oranges at their present price.

I understood my
right lion, friend to say that there were about one hundred oranges in a cubic foot, which would make the increase about one-third of one cent per orange. That is about the smallest possible recognition which could be given to empire oranges.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is my understanding of it.

I understand that these oranges are to be imported into Canada in wooden boxes and I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether the suggestion has been made to Australia that they use Canadian lumber in the manufacture of these boxes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I hasten to assure my
lion, friend that being wiser in our day and generation than were our predecessors, who did not include lumber in the last Australian treaty, the suggestion has been noted and I am happy to say that so far as may be reasonably possible, effect will be given to it.
My hon. friend will remember the feeling of resentment which was expressed by some Canadians who had purchased commodities produced within the British Empire and found that they were packed in boxes made of wood which came from Sweden. I assume that that is what my hon. friend had in mind when he made his observation.
What is the relative price of the best Australian and best Californian oranges?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The business in Australia has not been developed to proportions comparable to that of California, but during the past year or two Australia has been shipping some oranges into Canada. I understand that there is a shipment en route of some 15,000 boxes, and the price must have been below the California quotation in order to meet that competition. Australia feels quite confident that within the next year or two she can secure a very substantial portion of this business, and then there are South Africa, the West Indies and other sections of the British Empire to be considered. This is looked upon as being one of the most hopeful developments which might be expected from this treaty. It must be remembered-this will appeal particularly to some hon. members opposite-that some commodities from Australia must find access to this market. This is one of the items where there is a very good prospect for development.

I thank the Minister of
Trade and Commerce for his answers but I do not seem to get the information which I was desirous of securing with regard to the relative prices of Californian and Australian oranges. I understand he is unable to give it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I do not happen to have it under my hand.
Mr. EiLLIOTT: The great danger in connection with this is that we are imposing a duty of 35 cents per cubic foot on oranges and all we are going to be able to do is to increase the price by that amount to the consumer, not only on the oranges on which we collect a duty but on those that come in free. Is the Minister of Finance able to state whether or not in the different orange producing countries they have a system of grading similar, for instance, to our system of grading apples in boxes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
South Africa and Australia have perhaps gone further than most other countries with respect to grading. My hon.

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
friend will no doubt recall that in a grocery store in this city plums and peaches from South Africa were on sale during last winter and they arrived here in excellent condition.
When a box of oranges comes in from Australia or any other country, is it marked No. 1, No. 2 or No 3 in a way similar to that in which Canadian apples are marked when they are shipped?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is putting it too strongly to say that there is an exact comparison, but broadly speaking, sizes determine No. 1 or No. 2 or No. 3. There is a fair degree of uniformity, but I should not like to mislead my hon. friend by saying that there is any absolute uniformity as between the countries.

Could there be inserted in this clause a provision which would exempt oranges that go into the manufacture of marmalade? I have a telegram from a marmalade manufacturer in my riding, complaining of the additional cost to them of their raw material, that is, their oranges. I noted just a minute ago the minister mentioned that South African oranges were getting a market in Great Britain. This telegram reads:
New tariff on oranges if applied to Seville bitters is equivalent of reducing the import duty on orange marmalade from England by one-half cent a pound. This together with advantage English manufacturers have on buying sugar for export at two dollars and ten cents below Montreal prices and buying their containers at much lower prices than Canadian manufacturers as well as lower labour costs will prevent Canadian manufacturers from competing with English manufacturers in our own home market.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: My right hon. friend told me last night there was no marmalade coming in under the general tariff.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is no traceable quantity.
Marmalade under the preferential tariff is at the same rate as formerly?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes. This is a small part of the production of jams.

The item in the treaty
reads:
Free during the months of May, June, July, August, September and October: British preferential tariff during the other months of the year.
Would these oranges not come in free during the whole year under the British preferential tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That is quite true. The only answer is that we have undertaken with Australia to maintain that irrespective of what change, if any, we may make in the British preferential.

I quite realize, as I suppose all of us do, that in order to maintain or develop trade between this or other countries we must give a quid pro quo, and that possibly there is no more suitable commodity than oranges on which we can give a preference. I realize too, that this will bring about a substantial increase in our revenue, because the oranges will continue to come in and upon them that duty of approximately seventy-five cents a box must 'be paid. It is equally obvious that for some time at least, when you take into account the very large quantities imported from the United States, and the very small quantities imported from within the British Empire, this will mean simply an additional cost of these oranges in this country of about seventy-five cents a box, with, in all likelihood, an additional cost for orange marmalade or any kind of preserves made from oranges, because if the duty is not increased at the present time to meet the increased cost of the raw material, it will undoubtedly have to be increased in the near future. At this time when people find it so extremely difficult to pay for fruits or for fruit preserves at present prices, it seems rather deplorable that we are obliged to make a definite increase in the cost of that essential fruit and of the preserves made from it. Of course we cannot do anything about the matter. I realize we have to sacrifice something in order to obtain a market for some of our own goods, but again, just as has so frequently been the case, the result is that the general run of consumers-I am not speaking particularly now of the farmers -will simply have to pay a little more in order that certain industries may be able to climb on their shoulders over the tariff walls of other countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I might take a few
moments to draw the attention of the committee to the history of tariff as it relates to oranges. About twenty to twenty-five years ago Canada used to receive a very considerable portion of her supply of citrus fruits, chiefly oranges, from the West Indies and other countries. Then the Citrus Fruit Union of California was formed, and this citrus fruit union became a very highly developed and efficient organization. The formation of that organization and its control, through the tariff, of the United States market resulted in the destruction of citrus fruit production, as far as oranges are concerned, in the West Indies. Most of the growers there abandoned the production of oranges because they were denied access to the United States market, and as a result Canada suffered. The price of citrus fruit rose considerably and for twenty years or thereabouts it has been I think entirely under the dictation of the Citrus Fruit Union of California without any competition. All this time or most of it this same citrus fruit was on the free list so far as Canada was concerned-. The result to this country was the higher price that we have paid for the fruit. The standard price for lemons, for instance, a few years ago was 20 cents a dozen and less, while in recent years lemons have rarely dropped as low as 20 cents. I am not complaining; I am not criticizing the Citrus Fruit Union, but the effect on Canada was an increase in price. We believe that, not this year, perhaps not next year, but within a reasonable time, Australia, South Africa, probably all of the West Indies, and other parts of the British Empire, will again get into the citrus fruit business, and with a market such as we have to offer in Canada we really expect that as a result of this action the price of citrus fruit within the next few years will actually drop instead of being increased. I venture to say that even this year, at the commencement, when it is rather too much to expect it, there will really be no increase in prices.

I think that the
reason of that is that the duty is so small; it is less than one-third of a cent per orange. I am disposed to agree with the minister in this case, although I rarely agree with his deductions on tariffs, but in this case he happens to be Liberal, and I am nofgoing to oppose him.

I confess I cannot understand the wording of this item. It says free during the months of May, June, July, August, September and October, and the British 22110-238
preferential tariff during the other months of the year. Now the British preferential tariff is free, so I would take it that these oranges are to be free in May, June, July, August, September and October, and free during the rest of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I have already explained
that. We are giving to Australia a guarantee that as long as the treaty exists oranges shall be on the free list so far as Australia is concerned. At the present time we are leaving oranges free under the British preference, but it does not follow that they will always be free under the British preference. We will be at liberty to change the British preferential rate, but the rate for Australia will be free whatever we do with the British preference, with the limitation fixed in the treaty.
Then why insert that stipulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am afraid it must be
my fault or my hon. friend would have caught the point, because I have already explained it twice. At present oranges are free under the Australian treaty and under the British preference. We have undertaken with Australia to keep oranges free during certain specified months no matter what we may do to the British preference.
Why insert this stipulation if you have made them free for the whole year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I need hardly explain to
the hon. gentleman, with his well-known qualities of understanding, that during the other months of the year this parliament might make the British preference one cent. This provision ensures freedom of entry during the months mentioned whatever the British preference may be. It would not be correct to say, free the year round, for the British preference might not some day be free.

Speaking from memory it
seems to me that normally oranges are cheaper in the spring months, and if the government saw fit at some future time to impose a one cent duty under the British preference, we could surely let Australian oranges in free the year round.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They have not asked
for it.

This item contemplates that there are certain months of the year during which Australia is not anxious to furnish our requirements, and in the other months there will be a surplus. It is reasonable to

assume, if we give this advantage 'to Australia, that there should be storage facilities in Canada sufficient to take care of our requirements when Australia cannot supply them. Are the Australians contemplating providing storage facilities in Canada so that their oranges may be placed on the market evenly throughout the year, or if not, is the government contemplating any action to facilitate the marketing of these oranges, or will it be ldft in the hands of private importers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

Mr. MeMILLAN (Huron): You intend to leave it at five cents per pound?

Does this
apply to pineapple alone?

This is an increase?

Even to Australia?

Mr. MeMILLAN (Huron): I would like to know the reason for this.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Australian rate will be one cent, and in order to give them a preference the rate has been increased to other countries. The rate to other Countries being three cents, and the rate to Australia being one cent, there is a preference of two cents to Australia imder the British preferential tariff, three cents under the intermediate tariff, and four cents under the general tariff. On importations of pineapple from the United States, for instance, the preference in favour of Australia would be four cents, and under the intermediate tariff the preference would be one cent less than that. So far as other countries of the British Empire are concerned-this is one of the few items of which this may be said-^Australia gets a preference of two cents more per pound on pineapple than would be available to those other countries.
Where does it say that the Australian rate will be one cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
In the schedule to the
treaty, page 7.
Mr. STEW'ART (Edmonton): This is giving Australia a considerable preference over the other British dominions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it is. I thought my hon. friend would ask that question. It prob-xbly does not put them on an equality with their competitors in other British possessions, for the principal point of production of pineapples outside of Australia is Singapore in the Straits Settlements, from which considerable quantities are exported and where labour conditions are such that the cost of production is very much less than elsewhere. One might say that the native population there receives much less for its labour than does the population of'Australia.

Why not in that case make
pineapples free from Australia and place the general tariff at four cents? We do not produce pineapples; therefore why put a tax on them?

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff

I was just
going to suggest the same remedy. As we cannot produce pineapples, it seems to me that the duty should be very low, and if we propose to give Australia a preference over the other British dominions why not allow Australian pineapples to come in free?

speechtext:
It will be observed on
reference to the item that these are:
Fruits, prepared, in air-tight cans or other air-tight containers, the weight of the containers to be included in the weight for duty:

(b)	pineapples, 1 cent per pound;

There is a very considerable business done in Canada in canning pineapple.
Where?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: In Canada, a very substantial business. This tariff is to prevent that business being entirely destroyed, while at the same time affording the preference I have indicated to Australia over other competing countries, the particular country being that to which I have just referred, where the wages of the native population are so low that even other parts of the empire have found it necessary to have recourse to the tariff to afford them fair competition.

How are fresh pinapples
affected?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
They are not dealt with
at all. If my memory serves me aright, they are free.

Is any inquiry made by
the department with respect to the sanitary conditions under which pineapples are canned in the Straits Settlements? In this country we have very strict food and factory laws and our canning plants are frequently inspected by government officials. Yet, as I understand it, we allow canned goods to come into Canada without any knowledge at all of the conditions under which they are put up.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I always hesitate to bo
too critical with respect to conditions under which other countries cany on their business.
I am not criticizing, I am asking for information.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I have only said that I hesitate to be too critical with respect to it. My information is that some form of sanitary inspection is provided for by the laws of the 22110-238^
Straits Settlements, but that the factory conditions are not such as obtain in modern factories in Canada and elsewhere. Certainly it is wholly within the mark when one says that the wages and conditions of labour of the native population in that community are very different from the conditions of labour and wages that prevail in other countries where we have stringent pure food laws. There are factory regulations in force _ in most exporting parts of the British empire, but obviously in Singapore they have not reached the same advanced stage in their canning operations as would be expected under the wholly different habits and modes of life that prevail in this country.

speechtext:

satisfy the hon. gentleman that the course being taken is one which he himself would pursue. As a result of the action taken previously, three Canadian plants were closed and have not since operated. market is available, it will bo seen that we have at least taken the precaution to provide within our own boundaries for the production of a very necessary commodity without involving an increased price to the consumer.

Would the Prime Minister
tell me whether dry dusting materials are dutiable at the rate of 15 per cent, together with liquid preparations? They were classed with liquid preparations at the time the duty was taken off, if my memory is correct.

The hon. gentleman will

Could the minister give me
an idea of how important these factories are which were closed as a result of the duty being taken off, and how many hands they employed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Prior to 1928 these
arsenical insecticides were dutiable at 15 per cent, 171 per cent and 175 per cent, with others dutiable at 10 per cent, 15 per cent and 20 per cent. I have some knowledge of only about a half dozen of these factories; I am bound to say to my hon. friend that I could not give him even approximately the number of people who would be employed, but I am informed that a substantial number of people would find employment. They sent a delegation here; I took a statement, which was investigated; they were willing to undertake not to increase the price, and they realized what would be the result if that were done. They were all manufacturers of certain types of disinfectants or insecticides, but I think two of the factories had been closed for some two or three years. They were endeavouring to start up again with respect to another line and wanted also to be able to secure this production. I am inclined to think that under similar conditions the hon. gentleman would have adopted the same course.

I remember very distinctly the debate which took place when these articles were placed on the free list in 1928. Certain private members stated that factories would be adversely affected, and I tried to get an idea of how many people would be so affected, but was unable to do so. I formed the impression, perhaps wrongly, that the industries were not very important, and that is why I requested the information from the minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think I can procure some little information for my hon. friend at a later date. One of the hon. members has a very large plant of this character in his constituency, and I will communicate to my hon. friend the number of people employed there, though I believe I can give the details with reference to only two factories.

Does this refer to animal
dip, that is, sheep dip and cattle dip?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Any sort of dip; it is the same wording.

Has the right hon. gentleman received any representations from the Canadian wool growers' cooperative society with regard to the powder they use for dipping sheep? This powder is used all over Canada, and I should like to know whether the Prime Minister has been assured that a real substitute will be found for this preparation, which is called the Cooper dip powder. Has the minister received any representations from the wool growers' cooperative or the sheep breeders' association?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am bound to say no such representations have reached me, and I am told by the officials that no such communications have reached the department. I will make a note to make further investigation, but certainly I have no knowledge of it myself.
I should like to have this information, because this is a very important factor in sheep raising.

I want to place on record
my opposition to this item. I am opposed to it because in 1928, although it was stated that no difference would be made in the price when the duty was taken off, immediately after the duty was taken off the price of these spraying materials dropped in my constituency. Advertisements appeared in the local press offering spraying materials at considerably reduced prices. It is all very well for the Prime Minister to say that the price will not go up as a result of the duty. But it is going to be difficult for my constituents to keep a check on the prices. I shall do the best I can to keep a check on it myself, and if there is the slightest evidence of an increase in prices I will bring the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister. This is something of great importance to the people I represent, and before the item carries I want to have it recorded that I am opposed to it.

Through

I cannot
help thinking that those who will be affected will learn too late, to their sorrow, what has happened to them.

It is rather difficult to understand how it will be possible for those firms who have gone out of business to resume without increasing prices. Apparently they went out of business because they could not meet the prices. Is it expected that if the entire market is assured to them through a virtual monopoly they will be able to produce at a lower cost than they have been able to do? I cannot understand how they will be able to carry on, seeing that, unable to manufacture at present prices, they have been obliged to shut down.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The curtailed production has had the result I have indicated. One large firm had on hand a very considerable quantity of arsenate of lead which was used in the production of their commodity. When their business was curtailed, because of the circumstances to which I have alluded, they stopped operations. They still have that raw material and it is unimpaired; age has not affected it. They believe, as I do, that the increased production, resulting from a greater demand by reason of the domestic market being available, will ensure their being able to carry on their business. The hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) places altogether too modest a value upon his own resourcefulness, for I am satisfied that if his constituents are called upon to pay enhanced prices-barring, of course, an increase in raw material, for which he will always make allowance-it will not be very long thereafter before the government is made aware of the fact.

I trust that the Prime Minister's hopes will be realized and that the manufacturers will be able to carry on. But I understand that they ceased producing when imports began to come in under the
{Mr. list y.]
free list, because they could not meet the prices. I think it is rather doubtful that this tariff will enable them to carry on. It is an interesting experiment and-I have no axe to grind-I hope they will succeed.

The Prime Minister says
that the Canadian Horticultural Council passed a resolution or in some other way expressed themselves in favour of this increase. Has he a record of the stand they took?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

This question was considered at the annual meeting of the horticultural council. The fruit growers represented there by their delegates did not raise any objection to the increase in the protection on these spray materials for the special purpose of increasing production to meet their requirements.

Does this item include chemical sprays used for the killing of weeds? If it does I have strong representations from those who manufacture these chemicals. They say that the change is going to increase the cost of chemicals which are being tried out generally in the west by the municipalities for the destruction of weeds.

The hon. member for Yale
represents an important fruit growing constituency in British Columbia and he follows with great care the proceedings of the horticultural council. I have tried to do so myself, and I understand that what happened in the council this year was this. Certain members desired higher duties on apples and they felt that they would be hampered in their demand if they objected to higher duties on spraying materials. That is the reason for the stand they took. The hon. gentleman says they took that stand because they desired an increase in the production of these goods-

speechtext: In Canada.

-in Canada, yes. But I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me

I do not know where the hon. member met those individuals who desired a higher duty on apples. I have neveT met them.

There is no question about it that demands have been made for higher duties on apples. In the Halifax Herald of Monday, July 13, 1931, there appears a report to the effect that the government has placed higher duties on apples for the purpose of protecting the home market. There is a long despatch reporting the paternal and beneficial action which the government has taken in connection with this industry. There certainly was a demand. The hon. gentleman and I look on these matters from different points of view. I think a better policy for the apple industry would be to keep down costs of production and place such articles as spraying and dusting materials on the free list. That would be better than attempting to keep up the prices of the product by these high valuations for duty purposes and higher duties.

The hon. member for

I was referring to clocks.

clocks.

I think there are only two

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are three clock
factories in Canada, one at Peterborough, one at Kitchener, and I believe one at Brantford. The brief filed by the clock and watch parts makers-I refer now to the cheaper watch which is something like a clock-asked for an increase over the existing rate. When this item was published these manufacturers indicated that an upward change would be highly regarded, but the largest producer, whose operations run to something over 2,300 watches and clocks per day, thought it worth while to allow the item to stand for a year as it gave a much better rate than had existed previously. I think the considerations which moved us to make this change might well have moved my hon. friend when he had the chance of doing the same thing.

I had not the opportunity
of making a change. I understood that the small producers who have found considerable difficulty in meeting foreign competition were not satisfied and felt that the change did not do them very much good.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
What does the hon.
gentleman suggest?
I am not making any suggestion. I desire only to find out whether representations were made, and if so, what answer was given.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My memory is that one manufacturer said that he was pleased with 
the item and no further change was desired; another suggested an upward movement from 15 per cent to 27J per cent, and another suggested that the rate should be 30 per cent. As a matter of fact, the differentiation between parts and the finished product has been maintained. My personal view was that it might have been increased a little, but having regard to the reports of the industry generally, the changes should afford to Canada an opportunity to compete on fair terms against importations from at least the United States, and, I believe, from Germany. That is, I think, the representation that was most strongly made. I am speaking from memory and subject to correction.

It has always been represented that the purpose of protective tariffs was to foster new or, as they are so often called, struggling industries. If any industry could go into that category it would be the clock making industry. As I know from the experience of a factory in my own town, it had a struggle for many years. While I am not necessarily advocating, if the duty is regarded as sufficient, that it should be higher, it is still comparatively low, may I say to some of my hon. friends on this side, as compared with the tariff that has been given to what can hardly be described as infant industries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that clocks, time recorders, clock movements, clock-work mechanisms and clock cases are now 20 per cent, 30 per cent and 35 per cent. The general tariff of 35 per cent is, I think, a fairly reasonable one having regard to the information we had as to, shall I say, large capacity for production. I cannot recall that any communication came from the particular industry in Kitchener to which my hon. friend refers, but I shall endeavour to find out. during the recess if there has been any.
Can the minister give us any information as to what it costs to put a watch movement in a casing? How much labour is involved?
Every little movement has a meaning all its own.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That depends entirely on the character of the movement. If it is a highly jewelled movement of a certain type, it costs a substantial sum of money. Everything depends upon the skill and care that has to be exercised with respect to it. These fine watch cases are of course now made in Canada, as the hon. gentleman may know.

It depends upon the skill of the workman, the quality of the movement, and the fineness of the case. I could not give an estimate of the price.

As we are speaking about clocks and watches, this will perhaps be the proper time to ask the Prime Minister: How is it that all the requests of the manufacturers are listened to and complied with while the requests from the farmers are not heeded? Will the Prime Minister allow me to speak on the question of wool, in connection with which the farmers put forward very strong recommendations for a tariff?

Wool is a big item. It touches nearly all the farmers in Canada. 1 have had no opportunity of discussing this item, because it has not been called, but I remember very distinctly hearing the right hon. gentleman tell us last session that any of the items-

I rise simply to ask the Prime Minister if he will give me an opportunity of discussing this question of a tariff on wool.

I will ask the Prime Minister, who is so obliging-

Perhaps, Mr. Chairman,
you were not following the discussion last evening. I said very distinctly to my hon. friends opposite that by reason of what was said at the short session they might avail themselves of the opportunity to discuss any item that they desired to discuss. I understand that the hon. member for Kamouraska is instituting a comparison between the tariff items that touch industry and those that touch agriculture. I should think he would be within his rights, having regard to the arrangement that was made, in instituting such a comparison at this time.

I am grateful to the
Prime Minister for the permission he has just
given me. I am not a firm believer in high protection as a means of helping the farmers, but if the government is going to do something in regard to raising the tariff, whatever advantage may accrue to the farmers should be taken by them. I suppose the Prime Minister is aware of the many representations that were made through the Minister of Agriculture in regard to having a tariff on wool. Wool is imported in very large quantities, and I should like to quote from a letter addressed to the Minister of Agriculture under date of December 26, 1930, and signed by the manager of the Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers, Limited. I will read just the last paragraph of this letter. It states:
AVith the exception of carpet wools as described, all other wools imported into Canada, to all intents and purposes, may be described as competitive with Canadian grown wool, and any further exceptions would materially reduce any advantage to Canadian sheepmen in a general tariff on wool.
On the same date, the manager of the same cooperative wrote to the Minister of Agriculture another letter, and I am quoting just the fourth paragraph which states:
When talking with Mr. Breadner on Tuesday, he stated that any tariff legislation should be specified, and that such a basis for duty as 20 cents per pound of clean content, would leave the amount to be collected on wool in the grease variable. That is true, at the same time it seems to be worldng out satisfactorily in the United States, where they have wool appraisers for this work, and where each invoice on imported wool, bears the estimated shrinkage figures.
As explained to Mr. Breadner, if it was necessary to name a specific rate on wool in the grease, we would have to be guided by the 20 cent rate on clean scoured wool, using the shrinkage of 30 per cent which is the shrinkage on a large part of wrool imported into Canada. In other words, on this basis the duty on wool in the grease would be 14 cents per pound.
Later I wrote to Mr. George O'Brien, manager of the Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers, Limited, to ascertain what has taken place, and I received this letter dated June 30, 1931:
Dear Air. Bouchard:
We are in receipt of your message of June 26, and we are sending you copy of the letter sent the Hon. Mr. Weir, which contains insummary a report of the Sheep Conference in Toronto. AA7e also enclose copy of letter and brief filed at Ottaw'a with respect to wool. Our correspondence on this subject has been large, and we have included the Department of Agriculture, Department of Finance, , and Department of National Revenue.
AATe also took up the question of lamb and mutton, and that has been dealt with, though we are not informed at this time as to where these products stand in the new Australian trade agreement.

Toronto, March 26, 1931.
lion. Robert Weir.
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa.
Honourable Sir,-
At the conclusion of the annual meeting of the Canadian Co-operative Wool Growers Limited, held in Toronto on March 26, 1931, those in attendance went into special conference on problems relating to the Canadian sheep industry. There were present between fifty and sixty sheep farmers and ranchers from every province in the Dominion, representatives of the Dominion and provincial departments of agriculture, as well as representatives of the packing industry, live stock marketing and wool marketing organizations-a gathering that certainly represented a real cross-section of all the interests related to the sheep industry in this country.
A very full and free discussion was entered into by all present during the full afternoon and evening sessions, and it was pointed out that we are not producing nearly as much wool and lamb as we are using in this country, and that consequently there should be much room for expansion. It was unanimously agreed, though, that any such expansion was not possible on a profitable basis unless the home market was reserved and developed for Canadian producers by adequate protection on lamb, mutton and wool in all its forms.

speechtext: Without at all discussing the merits of the bill I should like to rise to a point of order to enable me to obtain your guidance, Mr. Speaker. It always has been allowed,
since we have been in the house; the member moving the second reading of a bill always has been allowed to speak in reply, I do not care what the rules are.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: NATURE OF SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Prior to 1927 what is
now standing order 43 was rule 21, subsection 2, and it contained the words "second reading of a bill." Standing order 43, citing the circumstances in which a member has the right of reply, did not include the words "the second reading of a bill" after the revision of the rules in 1927. This was not done with the idea of changing the rule, but because those words were considered superfluous. Notwithstanding what is stated in Campion, which I have examined, it has been the practice in this house to allow a reply on the second reading. subtopic: NATURE OF SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during several of the occasions devoted to private bills this measure has been under consideration, and I think it has been viewed from a number of different angles. I would point out that there has been a great deal of misunderstanding as to the purpose of the bill. There have been those who have taken the stand that it has to do with sedition, but the clauses in the criminal code having to do with sedition will remain untouched. If any man utters any seditious words he is still liable to be charged with sedition. My bill was simply intended to safeguard the right of free speech, because of certain practices which have grown up in a number of our cities during recent months.
There is little for me to add to what I said when introducing the bill. It has been said that the bill is poorly drawn. Let me say that I obtained the best legal advice available, not merely the advice we have at our disposal here but outside legal advice in drawing the bill, and the phraseology to which a great many of the legal members have objected is supplied by those who have had considerable experience with the law. I

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
remember very well a few months ago when a certain bill was 'before this house it was ridiculed by some members of the legal profession until they found that the draftsman was a man recognized as being in the very forefront of his profession. Ever since that time I have not had very much fear when presenting a matter like this, especially when I know it has been carefully prepared by a legal authority.
There was one point I should have liked to present earlier, and I think I shall add it now, because it seems to me to bear very directly upon the whole subject matter. I have reference to a decision appearing in the Ontario law reports, in the case of Rex vs. Patterson. It seems to me, if I may say so, looking at it from the layman's standpoint, that it is rather a serious blow at the freedom of the individual, and if this sort of thing is to go on unchecked we may find that our freedom of speech is curtailed. I shall read from the judgment of Middleton J.A., appearing in the Ontario law reports of December 11, 1930:
All this satisfies me that the accused was a member of an assembly, lawful in its inception, but unlawful in its execution, because it was determined to meet force by force and to resist the officers of the law. It is quite immaterial that the officers of the law may have been mistaken in their interpretation of the police regulation, or that the regulation itself may be invalid. This does not justify the use of force against constituted authority, or even against any other, to the disturbance of public peace. The conviction must be affirmed. I would commend the learned county court judge for his good sense and moderation in dealing with this case.
Mulock. C.J.O., and Grant. J.A., agreed with Middleton, J.A.
There are just two points I should like to mention, though perhaps the house will think I have considerable temerity in criticizing a judgment of this kind. I should like to direct attention to this sentence:
It is quite immaterial that the officers of the law may have been mistaken in their interpretation of the police regulation	
That is going altogether too far. It is a most dangerous position when the officers of the law are upheld even though they may be mistaken with regard to their interpretation of a police regulation. Then comes the second part of that sentence:
.... or that the regulation itself may be invalid.
Again I think we are proceeding on very dangerous ground. In this instance the trouble was that a group of citizens proceeded to have some sort of parade, thinking they

were quite within their rights. As a matter of fact they were not disobeying any police regulation, yet the officers told them to disperse. As was shown by the evidence, the officers had no right to interfere because the men who were on parade were not disobeying any police regulation whatever. The officers were entirely mistaken, and when these men stood on their rights as citizens and said they had a right to walk through the streets they were arrested by the police, who were upheld in their act. I say that sort of thing is dangerous to our citizenship. Then let me read from the minority judgment of Magee, J.A.:
This appellant, leading a peaceable procession, and said but not proved to have been acting in breach of some by-law, is arrested and, instead of being charged with breach of by-law, for which he might be fined, is charged with a crime for wdiich he might be imprisoned. The hands of our peace officers endeavouring to enforce the laws should be upheld and strengthened, but I am unable to convince myself that on the evidence here presented this conviction should stand, and therefore I would allow the appeal.
Then Fisher, J.A. said:
I fully agree with the conclusion of my brother Magee that this appeal should be allowed, and I desire to add that the crown has utterly failed to produce-as it was bound to-any witness proving that persons in the neighbourhood had reasonable grounds to fear that the peace would be disturbed tumultuously, or to provoke other persons to disturb the peace tumultuously.
The appeal was dismissed, Magee and Fisher dissenting. I thought it was well perhaps to add this Hamilton case which bears very directly on my contentions of a few weeks ago.
It chanced that in my presentation of the bill I mentioned the city of Toronto, and I instanced some of the practices of the police which I considered inimical to the maintenance of free speech. A number of hon. gentlemen from Toronto seemed to regard this as a direct attack on that city. That is not so. I also mentioned similar instances from the city of Montreal. I have just mentioned one that relates to Hamilton and I have mentioned some with regard to western Canada. But some of these gentleman seem to be very jealous of any criticism of Toronto. In fact, when the bill was last under discussion one hon. member declared that the city of Toronto did not need to be defended. He went on to speak of the admirable things that had been done in Toronto-the enormous amount given in Christmas relief and the sums contributed to the patriotic fund. Just what that has to do with the criminal code

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
I fail to see, but evidently he thought that something was needed to counterbalance the criticism of Toronto.
Now, I am a native of Toronto, so that I have nothing particularly against that city. My father and mother before me were natives of Toronto. I cannot therefore be regarded as altogether an outsider. But it does seem to me that in the last few years Toronto, more than any other city in Canada, has been adopting a great many of the most reprehensible practices which we read of as occurring in some of the larger eastern American cities. It is nothing to be proud of that these practices, which we denounce when we observe them in American cities, should be tolerated when they prevail in a city under the British flag. I should rather like to think that in advocating such measures as this we are in reality standing for the very best British traditions. I think we are. Unless I was entirely misled when I was a child, I was given to understand that Britain stood for freedom of speech. Yet I heard the other day one of those hon. members who are opposing this bill say that the people of Toronto do not believe in free speech. He gave as one evidence of this the fact that a very small number of electors had voted for a certain communist candidate. The hon. gentleman is confusing the idea of free speech with some sort of extravagance on the part of certain communists of Toronto.
I do not know that it is necessary for me again to dissociate myself from the communist party. Someone says it would not do me any good. That is a very smart remark. But let me say that if anyone would like to know how the communists regard me all he has to do is to read the columns of The Worker, the communist paper, or other communist publications circulated in the country. I am not a member of the communist party, but I do believe that we are in danger of being stampeded because of the prevalence of a number of communists in the country. And even though they opposed me and both my colleagues at the last election. I say none the less that I stand for free speech. It was only the other day when I was in the city of Windsor that a meeting which I was addressing was almost broken up by a group of communists. I do not like that kind of thing and I will not stand for it, because I believe that I should have the right to freedom of speech. If the trades and labour council call a meeting, as they did on that occasion, they should have the right to conduct that meeting without interruption by communists. That is only fair. But that is a different thing altogether from taking the ground that the communists have no right to speak in public or otherwise to voice their ideas. A number of the ideas of the communist party are not my ideas, but that does not mean to say that I should try to have them suppressed by force. If one set of opinions are suppressed by force it will be only a matter of time until other ideas are similarly suppressed. So that even though the communists are bitterly opposed to us we still stand for freedom of speech, and I trust that in this position we shall be joined by a great many other citizens.

speechtext:
I do not know
whether Quebec is any freer in this regard than Toronto, because in recent times the city police have been very active in Montreal with respect to the communists.
Since one or two other members have had so much to say with reference to communism, perhaps I may be permitted to add a few words on the subject, although it seems to me to be apart from the bill before us. Someone the other day said that the O.B.U. was the same thing as communism. I am not and never have been a member of the O.B.U., but I have had occasion in the last ten years to study closely the various labour organizations in this country, and the man who states that the O.B.U. and communism are one and the same thing is absolutely mistaken. The
O.B.U. is an organization in the industrial field. It was the result of an effort some years ago to get all the different trade unions into one large industrial body. It largely failed in its purpose although it is still in existence as an organization. But it was not a political organization at all, whereas communism is.
May I point out that however much some may dislike some of the doctrines of communism, there is after all no law in this country against it. It is not an illegitimate organization. Hence the communists ought to be allowed to carry on their meetings so long as they do not interfere with the freedom of others. If anyone is afraid of their talking sedition, the law is there and they can be prosecuted. Indeed, I often wonder why some of those who are opposed to the appearance of the oommunists in public do not adopt the reasonable course and charge them with sedition. The law, I say, is there and these people, if they preach sedition, can be dealt with under it.
It was only yesterday that my colleague from Vancouver called attention to still another infringement upon free speech. Accord-
3752	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
ing to our information a prominent medical man of the city of Vancouver, who is also a member of the independent labour party, has been broadcasting. Some of the people in Vancouver did not like what he was saying, but a great many did. A complaint was made to the broadcasing company as well as to the department at Victoria. I have not as yet received the papers which would give me an accurate account of Avhat took place or just who is to blame, but this doctor has been notified that he can no longer broadcast over this particular station. Here seems to me to be another danger to freedom of speech. When a broadcasting station is given a licence by the Department of Marine and Fisheries it has a certain general duty toward the public. If any man is willing to pay for the right of broadcasting he should be permitted to do so.
