speechtext:
Doctor Lyle Telford. I am just instancing this as being another instance of the curtailment of free speech. If this kind of thing is permitted it would mean that this new instrument for publicity, the radio, would be in the hands of a few, and if that few did not like what was being said or did not like the particular political doctrine which was being taught, they could suppress that speech and prevent that individual from giving any more broadcasts. To adopt that principle is to relinquish all our British ideals of freedom of speech.
There are laws against sedition, which laws can be invoked at any time. A man can be charged, regularly tried and convicted, and that is the proper method to pursue. We ought not to have a censorship such as some of our cities have been seeking to set up.
Regarding some of the charges made against the police of Toronto, let me direct attention to the fact that the hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) confessed that intimidation had been used in connection with the rental of halls in the city of Toronto. I

know from those who have attempted to rent halls that; that has been the case, that the hall owners have been told that if they permitted such and such an organization to rent their halls they would have their licences cancelled. When I presented this bill I instanced a number of cases in which that action was taken within recent months. I say that that is an unwarranted extension of the licensing powers of the police and a distinct curtailment of freedom of speech..
All I am asking for in this legislation is that certain safeguards should be set up which would give the citizens a right to free speech so long as he did not violate the law. Hon. members say that they are quite willing to have free speech within the law; that is all I am asking for. If he goes outside the law the man who is guilty can be prosecuted; all we are asking for is free speech within the law. Just how far this restriction of freedom affects organizations other than the communist organization was made quite evident in the case of the Fellowship of Reconciliation, whose only crime was that they wanted to hold a meeting in the advocacy of free speech. They were not tiying to propagate the principles of communism, although that would not have been a crime; all they wanted to do was to hold a meeting in the advocacy of free speech, but they were prevented from obtaining a hall. I do not believe that such action is in the best interests of the people of this country.
This bill simply provides for the general right to assemble; it insists that before action can be taken there must be a danger of an immediate breach of the peace; that in judging of the character of the speeches an isolated word or phrase is not to be taken, but that the speech must be judged according to its general nature and character, and that the people called upon so to judge shall be firm and reasonable persons. The last phrase provoked a good deal of ridicule, the suggestion being made that there were no such people in the city of Toronto and that we would have to import them from other parts of the country. That particular phrase was taken from a judgment closely connected with this matter. I would not have chosen those words myself; I adopted them because of the legal advice which I had to the effect that they followed very closely a precedent in this regard. I am not seeking in any way to throw open the doors for seditious speech, I ask only, as is stated in the explanatory note, to provide a safeguarding clause to ensure that the general nature and character of speeches upon public affairs must be the

ground for regarding any meeting as unlawful. Surely we are in line with the very best British traditions when we insist that whatever else happens in this country, in times of peace at least, we must preserve the fullest freedom of speech and assembly.

When the committee
rose at six o'clock I was, through the courtesy of the Minister of Finance, discussing the question of wool. I do not desire to detain the committee much longer, but I should like to finish the letter I was reading. It continues:
The opinion was very freely expressed that such nurturing of the industry would result in higher grade produce and the introduction of sheep upon more of our farms. The necessity of some means of grading lamb and mutton was also strongly emphasized as an inducement towards better produce and as an assurance to the public of quality, resulting in greater consumption.
The following resolutions were accordingly drafted and unanimously agred upon:-
This meeting, called in conference on the sheep industry in Canada, with representatives of the producers of wool and mutton from every province in the Dominion, urges upon the government the necessity of the home market for their products, by means of a duty on all lamb and mutton, and a duty on the complete wool schedule from wool in the grease to yarns, and all waste therefrom, rags and shoddy. This duty to be sufficiently high to ensure to the producers a reasonable profit over and above cost of production.
These last few words would seem to anticipate what we find in the tariff board bill. The report on this meeting is headed:
Home Market Sought By Canadian Sheep Men
Ask Ottawa for safeguards against imports of wool and lamb-general conference follows annual meeting of Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers.
I will quote just a few sentences:
Preservation of the home market for Canadian grown lamb and wool was requested of the federal authorities at Ottawa in a resolution passed at the sheep conference which followed the annual meeting of the Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers in Toronto on March 26. Taking advantage of the presence of sheep raisers from all over the Dominion as well as representatives from the provincial and federal departments of agriculture, the packers, and others who attended the meeting of the cooperative, after the regular business, general questions were discussed and progress made in defining a sheep policy for Canada. It was pointed out that as we are not producing nearly as much wool and lamb as we are using in this country there was much room for expansion; that such expansion would be of great benefit in promoting sound mixed farming, but that unless the home market was reserved and developed for Canadian producers of lamb, mutton and wool in all forms, to ensure a reasonable profit over the cost of production, satisfactory progress could not be expected.
Just recently, on July 2, I received a letter which was forwarded to me by Mr. O'Brien, manager of the Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers, Limited, giving a little brief in regard to this question. This is the concluding portion:
Current wool prices to the grower in comparison with prices on white wool blankets at wholesale mill prices of 83 cents per pound f.o.b. Canadian mills, enjoying protection under British preferential tariff of 221 per cent plus 20 cents per pound, give a true picture to the present position of Canadian grown wool.
May I quote from the general report of the last meeting of the Canadian Cooperative Wool Growers, Limited, held at Toronto on March 26:
In this connection it was encouraging to note the following editorial comment in a recent issue of the Canadian Textile Journal. It read: "Once development of the woollen industry is based upon development and expansion of domestic wool production it will be on firm ground, and we believe this can be accomplished over a period of five years without added cost of either mutton or wool clothing to the consumer."
The president of the Canadian cooperative concludes as follows:
We appreciate this note of encouragement and cooperation from our textile friends.
At the end of this convention, the Toronto Daily Star came out with an interview headed:
Ask Bennett's help in wool distributing.

speechtext:
I ruled before that the hon. gentleman was out of order in discussing an item not before the chair. I have ruled before that any newspaper comment on the debate is out of order.

May I say that according to this editorial the tariff board under the Liberal regime had promised a duty on wool? I will conclude by saying this: If I crave the indulgence of the committee to speak on this question, it is because in the Dunning budget there was a tariff of 35 per cent on woollen fabric. But when we come to the drastic changes that took place in the tariff last fall, we find under the item 554b, "woven fabric composed wholly or in part of yarn or wool or hair" and so on, a general tariff of 40 per cent, or an increase of 5 per cent; but in addition to this we have an additional specific duty of 35 cents a pound under the British preferential tariff; 30 cents a pound under the intermediate tariff; and 35 cents per pound under the general tariff. This is an additional specific duty which to my mind is to bake care of a tariff that should have been put on wool. When I look up the United States tariff, I see that item 1108 covering woollen fabric, and so on, carries a duty of 50 cents per pound as a specific tariff, and 50 per cent ad valorem duty. I understand tkat the 50 cents per pound is imposed to take care of the tariff on raw wool. The inconsistency in our tariff is this, that you had a specific duty of 35 cents per pound on woven fabrics to take care of the tariff on wool in the fabric, but you have no tariff on raw wool. I shall not press this matter any further at the moment, but I draw it to the attention of the Finance minister in the hope that this question will receive further consideration when the new tariff board is functioning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was agreed, Mr. Chairman, that there should be an opportunity afforded for general discussion with respect to the items that were, in the view of my hon. friends opposite, but very inadequately discussed in the September session; hence the observations of the hon. member for Kamouraska, (Mr. Bouchard). May I say to him that he has overlooked just one factor with respect to wool, and it is the vital factor in determining the action of governments. It was the vital factor in determining that no action was taken by the tariff board.
This country has fewer sheep in it to-day than it had, say, twenty-five or thirty years ago. The entire number of sheep in Canada in 1928 was 3,415,000, and in the year 1871 the number was 3,153,000. The increase has not been at all commensurate with the demands. For instance, the entire wool production in this country is somewhere in the vicinity of 22,000,000 pounds a year, and the actual consumption of wool approximates 80,-
[The Chairman.]
000,000 pounds. Part of the reason why there is an importation of wool is that the wool thus far produced in this country is not suitable for the purpose of producing the quality of cloth that is sought. In other words, in any event, with the wool we are now producing in this country, it would be essential to import wool from Australia, New Zealand or some other country.
The question is, what action can be taken to ensure (a) an increase in the number of sheep in this country, and (b) such a quality of wool as would ensure the production of a sufficient quantity to meet in the main the requirements of this country. I need hardly say to the hon. gentleman that the problem during the short period in which this government has been in power has engaged its serious attention. If during the nine years he was content to support the government of that day he can point to any action taken by that government which increased the production of wool or of sheep in Canada, I shall be glad to hear of it. No such action was taken. The sheep industry has undoubtedly suffered in Canada.
I need hardly say that we propose, if we arc allowed a reasonable time within which to take action, to see that that state of affairs does not continue. One would think from such observations as those to which we have just listened that there had never been an opportunity afforded to the party to which he belongs to effect any of the reforms to which he refers. You would think they had been in the cold shades of opposition all their lives, and that this government had had for years and years an opportunity to effect the reforms which were much needed, and which are now rapidly being effected. I have not the slightest doubt in the world that when this matter has been carefully studied and all its implications are understood, we shall be able to devise a remedy to meet the situation. The reason that the duties were imposed upon the products of wool, namely, cloth and woollen goods, was that at the moment our factories and mills were closed absolutely by reason of the action taken by the preceding government, and we had either to stimulate and secure an industry that should be indigenous to this country, namely, the woollen industry, or let it perish. We took the course indicated by the schedules of last year, and if the hon. gentleman will give us, not as long as nine years, but half that time, he will find that the number of sheep in this country will have greatly increased, and that the production of wool will have been greatly adavanced, and we shall be producing the raw material from which our cloths are made to an extent that

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
we have not heretofore done. No animal is more valuable than the sheep to a farming country such as this, and perhaps there is no country in the world where sheep could flourish more profitably than in some parts of Canada. The sheep is valuable alike for its wool and for the food value of its meat. The sheep is one of the most productive of the animals upon farms. The records are clear upon that point. The sheep enriches the soil upon which it flourishes. It serves the agriculturist for food and clothing. To the extent that legislative action may stimulate that industry it will be taken, but may I say to the hon. gentleman that had he in the first year he came to this parliament to support the government of that day shown the zeal for the industry that he exhibits to-night, we might have hoped for some little reform on the part of the government which he supported.

I think I can show where there is a vast difference between conditions to-day and conditions when we were in power with respect to wool and the woollen industry. Go back to last September. I have not the tariff before me, but my recollection is that the tariffs were put up 35 and 40 per cent. That was on behalf of inter-imperial trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: On behalf of the woollen industry of Canada.

The Liberal policy on wool has always been to give the poor people, especially in the northern part of this country, woollen goods as cheaply as possible consistent with quality. That has been our policy, and the farmers were always, willing up to recently to produce their wool free in order to make their contribution towards free woollen fabrics. But now it is a horse of a different colour altogether. We have woollen goods coming into this country now under a duty of 40 per cent, shutting out the cheap woollen goods that we have enjoyed during all these past years. Why should the farmer be expected to make a sacrifice on behalf of free wool when the woollen manufacturers are getting 40 per cent protection, which is the position to-day? So far as I am concerned I am still in favour of free wool, and I would rather see the duty on the manufactured article put back to where it was, so that our people could get cheap woollen goods, than have further sacrifices made by the farmers in supplying free wool, while the manufacturers are getting 40 per cent protection. That is going a bit too far in discriminating against the various 22110-239
classes in Canada, and I am not surprised that the hon. member for Kamouraska is struck by the disparity.

Wool, namely, Leicester, Cotswold, Lincolnshire, Southdown combing wools, or wools known as lustre wools and other like combing wools, such as are grown in Canada:

What is the finished article of one industry may be the raw material of another, and at Ojibway they only process this finished article which they import as raw material. They do nothing but dip it, and thereby they ' get their tin plate.
It is said that these people have pledged themselves not to increase the price. Let me point out that the price has been increased, and in addition to the increase in price the maritimes are discriminated against in connection with freight rates as well. This tin is purchased in boxes weighing 112 pounds; the plates are generally 14 by 20 inches, weighing about 100 pounds per box. In 1929 the f.o.b. price at Pittsburgh, from which place this raw material is exported to Canada to be dipped and called tin plate, was $4.03 per box, and in 1930 it was 84.35. That was the price in the world market, where we were buying our supplies. The duty on that purchase now will be 64 cents. The Prime Minister a few moments ago made a statement which I think is correct, that in every part of the house we are in favour of the maintenance of an automobile industry in this country. There is no difference of opinion as to that. But there may be a distinct difference of opinion as to the measures which are necessary for the maintenance of that industry. A substantial increase in protection is given by these tariff resolutions, not so much by way of the tariff itself but by way of valuation and of free imports of certain parts-which lower the cost of construction to the manufacturer but do not necessarily cheapen the cost of the car to the consumer, because that again is set by competition from the outside. To my mind any increased protection to this industry might very properly have been left over until the new tariff board was functioning, because it is an industry which we cannot 
say is suffering intensely at the present time, and its condition vitally affects everyone in Canada.
I should like to make an observation while I am on my feet-an observation that I have thought of making a number of times. This session I have never criticized the government for their tariff policy. I made the statement on one occasion that undoubtedly the government did come into power on the pledge of increased protection. I for one have no criticism to offer with resepct to that increased protection, although I disagree as to its effect on the country. I think it is fair to say, speaking for the farmers of my part of the country, that they are not desirous of seeing any manufacturing industry suffer. They are willing to stand for a good deal to keep every industry running in such a way as to ensure employment to Canadian working men. The average farmer thinks-and it_is difficult to convince him that he is wrong -that during this period of depression almost every industry and every activity in the country has the shock to some extent Boftened by legislation-every industry except the farming industry. The manufacturing industry has its prices safeguarded, as far as they can be safeguarded, by protective tariffs. I will admit at once that the difficulty of selling their goods to a limited market has caused them troublous times, and I do not say they are making profits now; but I do say that so far as we can do so by tariff legislation we are protecting them from the shock of this depression and making certain, as far as it is possible, that they shall sell their goods at profitable prices. In the same way transportation service is protected under the Railway Act, and it is administered to ensure that no matter what the value of the products they cany the railways shall at least receive profitable freight rates. Likewise our banks, our mortgage companies and our loan companies are safeguarded by law so that they may be able to conduct their operations on a profitable basis. But what about the farmer? He says, and very logically, that he is left unprotected to bear the shock of this depression. I say unprotected, because although this government is doing its best to protect our farmers, no one knows better than the Prime Minister that the tariff has been of very little benefit to them. The farmer is willing to bear his share of the depression, to tighten up his belt and fight his way through, but he does feel that so far as it can be fairly done every class in the country should bear its fair share of the burden with him, otherwise he will be overwhelmed.

SI,000	would be 30 per cent. The importer of that car would pay to the manufacturer in the United States $700. When he brings that car to the border the duty at 20 per cent would be 8140. The order in council says he must not accept a 30 per cent discount, but is restricted to a 20 per cent discount; it says therefore that the valuation of that car for duty purposes must be $800. It is valued at $800, and the duty being 20 per cent he pays $160 in duty. Very well; then the customs official comes to him and asks, "What did you actually pay the manufacturer for the car?" If he says, "I paid $800," the official will say, "Very well; you have paid the proper duty". If, on the other hand, he says, "I paid only $700," the official will pay to him, "You have violated the dumping laws of this country, and now we will fine you the extra $100 which you did not pay for the car." If the purchaser says, "May I pay that $100 to the manufacturer and so get away without paying the $160 duty?" He will be told that he can do so. What will be his decision? He has the choice of paying that $100 either to his principal in the United States or into the public treasury here in the form of a fine. Undoubtedly he will pay it to his principal in
the United States, and the result of this order in council will be to transfer revenue to the pockets of the American manufacturer which might have come into the treasury of this country.

I would not further prolong the debate at this late stage of the session were it not for the reference made by the Prime Minister to the large amount of foreign capital invested in the automobile industry in Canada which he said it was our duty to protect. I should- like to direct the attention of the government to the statement contained in Hansard of March 29, 1926, in regard to the capitalization of the Ford Motor Company of Canada. It is shown that the original capital stock of this company amounted to $125,000, of which half, or $62,500, went to the Detroit company for certain rights they possessed. In 1926 the capital of the Ford Motor Company had increased to $7,000,000. No new capital had been put in; the balance of that $7,000,000 was taken from the profits which had been earned by the industry itself. A statement appearing in an article in the Financial Post of February 12, 1926, shows very clearly that all the capital stock of $7,000,000, with ithe exception of 8125,000, was earned out of the profits of the industry, and at that time the company's balance sheet showed a total net worth of $41,000,000. I think that company has done exceptionally well in building up a total net worth of $41,000,000 from an investment of $125,000, half of which was foreign capital.
Perhaps we are unduly alarmed with regard to the necessity of seeing that profits are returned on all this capital. Although this situation may seem satisfactory to the Prime Minister and the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), I believe the farmers of Canada are getting a little weary of maintaining this industry if it is to cost us as much as it has cost up to the present; for it takes seven steers at Chicago prices to buy a truck at Detroit prices, and eleven steers at Toronto prices to buy a truck at that point, and the difference is even greater when it comes to a sedan. The increased percentage of farm products necessary to purchase a car in Canada applies to many other commodities than steers; I think it would apply to butter, eggs, wheat and many other things. This is the problem facing the farmer, and it is a problem which the government must recognize. How can they increase the return to the farmer so that he may pay these increased prices?

The hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Young) has made a statement which I am sure was made in good faith but which I hope is not founded on fact. He claims that the 20 per cent discount works out in this way: We will say a car comes in on which the exporter in the United States allows a bona fide discount of 30 per cent. The department here allows a discount of only 20 per cent, and if the United States manufacturer does not actually sell his car on the basis of the 20 per cent discount the statement is made by the hon. member for Weyburn that the department applies the dump. Under the old administration of course that would have been quite impossible and quite unfair, because the dump is never applied unless the selling price in Canada is less than in the country of origin. I should like to know whether there has been any change in practice in that regard. If there has been a change and the dump is applied in a case like that I think it is an injustice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
When I heard the hon. gentleman make that statement my belief was that he was in error as to the application of the dumping clause. I am informed that it does not apply, and that he is wrong.
May I say to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that for the first time in the history of the country an earnest effort has been made to make an adjustment between the farmer's production and what he may pay with respect to duties and tariffs. Even if he has a unit as small as a quarter-section of land on which he produces 1,000 bushels of grain he would get $50, which at least is some compensating adjustment since it is more than he will have paid with respect to customs duties. From whom does that money come, primarily and principally it comes from these very industries to which we are referring, from the men whom he says we cannot longer keep but who are not asking to be kept. That is unfair and unjust, and is not advancing the cause of those whom I think other people have at heart quite as much as those who talk so much about it when they say the farmer is always the man who is being held up. The farmer is being given a compensating adjustment which more than meets the sum which on the average he will pay in duties with respect to motor ears or any other items of this nature with respect to t'he tariff.
I think he has already paid it.

If, as the minister says, this dumping duty is not applied to the man who

buys his car for $700 instead of for $800, which he should pay under the regulation, then I ask the minister how he enforces his order in council.

If that were true; if the automobile firms in the United States were making an extra $100 on each car, how would the hon. gentleman account for the fact that the Reo, the Graham, the Hupmobile and the Studebaker companies are all opening factories on this side of the line? Surely they would take advantage of that opportunity to make money. This legislation has forced these people to come over here and employ men on this side of the line, so that should be sufficient answer without going further into the matter.

I have not had any communications with automobile manufacturers in the United States, but I have received a communication from a manufacturer of cartridges, which have been treated in a similar way. This manufacturer asks, "Why am I compelled by your Customs department to charge my Canadian dealers 10 per cent more for cartridges than I am willing to accept from them or than I am charging my American dealers?" The same thing applies to automobiles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not accurate to-day.
When did it cease to be accurate?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Some time ago.

I should like to refer to item 1055, which states in part:
Provided, further, that no drawback shall be paid under this item on importations of any of the undermentioned articles.
Then follows a long list of articles on which under the old system no drawback was supposed to be allowed. With respect to the articles I shall mention, namely, a clutch, a universal joint, a transmission or a starting unit, I want to ask the Prime Minister what drawback is to be given. On what parts of these units is a drawback now to be given? Is it to be. given on the parts thereof or on the material therein? If on the parts, I can say that if a drawback is to be allowed on parts of universal joints then there is no necessity for putting that there at all, for the reason that 95 per cent of that article is in parts. Every one can be imported as a part, and if they are to have a drawback they have no right to be there. It was understood that these articles were not to have a drawback at all. That was my understanding

What is the answer?
Mr, BENNETT: The answer is there; they are on the exempted list.
I know it read's that way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman using the votes and proceedings of yesterday or of to-day?

I am reading from the votes and proceedings of yesterday, and I find in regard to the third item the following:
Provided, further, that on all materials and parts used in the manufacture in Canada of the parts enumerated in proviso (2) to the item there shall be payable, when such parts are used in the manufacture of the goods enumerated in tariff items 438a and 438b, a drawback of duty for domestic purposes of 25 per cent.
I wish the minister would be kind enough to explain 'that. I know what it means, and perhaps he will confirm my understanding * of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It means exactly what it says. There can be no misunderstanding of the language. At page 5 of the votes and proceedings of yesterday there appears the item, "materials and parts, n.o.p."; and, subject to drawback:
When used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff items 438a and 438b: 60 per cent.
Then:	[DOT]
Materials and parts, as hereunder defined, including all materials or parts wrought into or attached thereto; engines, bodies in the white. . . .
When used in the manufacture of goods enumerated in tariff items 438a and 438b: 25 per cent.
Then there is the proviso:
(1)	Provided, that no drawback shall hereafter be paid under this item unless at least 50 per centum of the cost of producing the finished article, not to include, after September 30, 1931, duties paid upon imported materials, has been incurred in Canada;
(2)	Provided, further, that no drawback shall be paid under this item on importations of any of the undermentioned articles.
And among those articles are universal joints.
Is there any drawback to be paid on the parts of universal joints?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The proviso is:
Provided, further, that on all materials and parts used in the manufacture in Canada of the parts enumerated in proviso (2) to the item there shall be payable, when such parts are used in the manufacture of the goods enumerated in tariff items 438a and 438b, a drawback of duty for domestic purposes of 25 per cent.

So far as that is concerned, I can tell the minister this, that all a man has to do in respect to universal joints is to put up a bench that will cost ten cents and bring these parts in and he can get the 25 per cent drawback. He does not need a factory or anything of that kind. And the same thing applies to all those other articles I have mentioned, such as transmission, clutches, axles, and so on. By having that drawback you prevent the main articles from being made in the steel mills of Canada.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Perhaps it might be well for me to summarize briefly the operations of my department since I took charge of it. I hope that these remarks will prove to hon. members on both sides that my desire has been to administer this department with economy but at the same time to give good administration and meet the urgent needs of the
Supply-Post Office

public. There must also be taken into consideration the general financial condition of the country. The deficit which has occurred in the department is due to the decrease of revenue brought about by the crisis affecting this and other countries of the world, while the increase in expenditure is caused by the obligations for the development of service imposed upon the department by the former administration and authorized by previous parliaments.
The deficit for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1931, is estimated at $5,293,000. The estimated expenditure for that year is $36,292,603, while the estimated revenue is placed at $31,000,000. In 1927-28 the expenditure amounted to $32,379,195, an increase of $1,371,497. In 1928-29, the expenditure amounted to $33,483,058, an increase of $1,103,863.
The hon. minister is referring to net revenue, not gross?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The increase in expenditure in 1930-31 is about $300,000 less than the increase in 1929-30. The increase in 1930-31 is estimated at $1,255,974, almost $800,000 of which is due to air mail service. The balance of the increase is due to the fact that the facilities accorded to the public were not curtailed. Notwithstanding the decrease in revenue, all services have been maintained, existing services have been extended and new services inaugurated. The increase in expenditure cannot be said to be due to the present administration but rather to the extensive nature of the service accorded to the public.
The present indications are that the revenue in 1930-31 will be approximately $31,000,000, a decrease of almost $2,000,000 as compared with 1929-30. In 1915 the postage rate on letters, other than for local delivery, was raised from two to three cents. This one cent tax resulted in a net increase in revenue amounting to about $3,000,000. In 1926 the war tax was removed from letters other than local which caused a loss of revenue amounting to about $2,600,000. At the same time the postage rate on letters to Great Britain and other parts of the empire was reduced from four to three cents.
Not at the same time.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
That is my information, but this matter can be discussed when we are taking up the details. In 1928 the source ol postal revenue was again reduced when the rate on letters within the British Empire was changed from three to two cents. On July 1, 1930, the rate on letters to certain countries within the International Postal Union was
[Mr. Sauve.l
reduced from eight to five cents. It will be seen that during the last few years several inroads have been made on the sources of postal revenue. Notwithstanding these reductions in postage rates, thereby diminishing postal revenue, the department has been obliged to maintain satisfactory services, extend existing services and establish new facilities, thus increasing expenditure.
The Post Office estimates show a decrease of $1,372,017.58. Part of this decrease is made up in salaries and allowances made possible by deleting for the present positions which have been vacant for some time and by decreasing the amount of mileage allowance made to railway mail clerks and the amount for temporary assistants. The reduction in. salaries and allowances will not mean that post office employees will be released. The reduction in mail service amounts to over $700,000, $412,000 being in the air mail.
The vote for miscellaneous expenditures has been reduced by $427,123.18. These reductions naturally preclude the possibility of general expansion or development of existing services, or the inauguration of new services, but with extremely economical administration we hope to maintain an efficient and satisfactory service, and at the same time to keep expenditure within the vote.
Salaries and allowances have been decreased by 8237,894.40. This is made possible by:
1.	Deleting provision for 366 positions in post offices and sixty-two railway mail clerkships which have been vacant for some time. Employees who are placed on the retired list or who leave the service for other reasons will not be replaced unless absolutely necessary.
2.	Reducing amount for temporary assistance by $120,000. This means that temporary employees will be taken on only in emergencies.
3.	Reducing amount for mileage allowance by $35,000. This is made possible by a reduction in personnel, pooling of crews of railway post offices and close supervision of assignments. No change has been made in the rate of mileage allowed railway mail clerks.
In the mail service the total decrease is $707,090. In the railway mail service the decrease amounts to $150,000. This is the result . of a rearrangement of mail services and railway train schedules as weil as close supervision of space units; in addition, no new services will be established. The reduction in the steamboat service amounts to $45,000. This is due to a falling off in mails offered for transportation on both the Atlantic and the . Pacific services. As regards the ordinary land service, including rural mail deliver}', there

Australian Trade Agreement
is no change. The vote in 1930-31 was $6,625,000 and the same amount is asked for 1931-32. While no curtailment will be made in the present services, the department will be unable to provide new services or to make extensions in existing ones. In the air mail service the reduction is $412,000. The general policy in regard to air mail is as follows: Air mail to outlying districts is a permanent feature of the departments policy. As regards all other air mail the government has considered it necessary to review the situation and to institute economies. In regard to the supply and repair of mail bags, the reduction amounts to $100,000. This is the result of economy in the use of mail bags, the purchase of a supply of cotton duck for letter bags being unnecessary for the reason that red striped bags formerly used for registered mail are being converted for use of ordinary letter mail and again placed in service.
In miscellaneous expenditure there is a decrease of $427,123.18. This is made up of a decrease of $5,000 in travelling expenses, $375,023.18 in stationery and printing, $40,000 in stamps, et cetera, and appropriations not [DOT] required for 1931-32, $6,500.
I think these explanations will satisfy my hon. friends opposite and also the committee in general.

I am a little surprised,
though perhaps I should not be, that the new minister, the first time he deals with his estimates, should take advantage of the item under civil government to give an apercu of the work of his department. The questions he has discussed have nothing whatever to do with civil government. If he had commenced with the estimates of the Post Office outside service, the rather full explanation he has given would have had its place or raison d'etre. I did not desire, as the hon. member is a new minister, to raise the point of order that he has taken advantage of the civil government item to give this explanation, but under this item it is impossible, according to the rules of the house, for me to discuss the department in general or the report laid before the committee by the minister. It is now approaching eleven o'clock. I have no objection to the item under civil government being adopted to-night, but when the first item of the outside service is called I expect to have the privilege of replying to the statement made by the minister to-night. As one who is perhaps supposed to take a greater interest in the Post Office Department than other members on this side of the house, I will claim that privilege when we reach the items of the outside service.
How many office appliance operators have you in the department?

speechtext: There are 107.
